M1: The wreckage of a star seen exploding in 1054 and recorded by Chinese and Japanese astronomers. What is left at the centre is a pulsar spinning thirty times a second.
M2: One of the richer and more compact globular clusters, and an old one even by the standards of its kind.
M3: A globular cluster of several hundred thousand stars, and the richest hunting ground for variable stars of any cluster in the sky.
M4: One of the nearest globular clusters, which is why it resolves into stars so easily. A distinctive bar of brighter stars runs across its middle.
M5: Among the oldest objects in the galaxy, and one of the finest globulars for a small telescope.
M6: The Butterfly Cluster, whose brighter stars trace a pair of open wings. Most are hot and blue, but the brightest is an orange giant.
M7: Ptolemy noted this cluster in the second century, which makes it one of the oldest recorded deep sky objects. It is an easy naked eye patch in a rich part of the Milky Way.
M8: The Lagoon Nebula, a vast star forming cloud split by a dark lane. At its heart is the Hourglass, a knot of gas being carved out by a single hot young star.
M9: A globular cluster near the galactic centre, dimmed and reddened by the dust lying between us and it.
M10: A bright globular cluster, and a close pair in the sky with M12 despite the two being nowhere near each other in space.
M11: The Wild Duck Cluster, one of the richest and most compact open clusters known, with a wedge of brighter stars that gave it its name.
M12: A looser globular than its neighbour M10, so loose that it was once taken for a dense open cluster.
M13: The great cluster in Hercules, the finest globular in northern skies. The Arecibo message was aimed at it in 1974.
M14: A globular cluster whose stars are faint enough to need real aperture before it resolves.
M15: One of the densest globulars known, with a core that has collapsed in on itself. It also holds a planetary nebula, which is very rare in a cluster.
M16: The Eagle Nebula, wrapped around a young cluster. Its towers of cold gas are the Pillars of Creation, and stars are still forming inside them.
M17: The Omega Nebula, also called the Swan. One of the brightest and most active star forming regions in the sky.
M18: A small, sparse open cluster of young stars, sitting between the Omega Nebula and the Sagittarius Star Cloud.
M19: One of the most oblate globular clusters known, squashed by the pull of the galactic centre it sits close to.
M20: The Trifid Nebula, named for the dark lanes that cut it into three. Red emission and blue reflection sit side by side, which is unusual and makes it a favourite.
M21: A young open cluster beside the Trifid, though the two are only neighbours in the sky.
M22: One of the brightest globular clusters in the sky and among the nearest, easily resolved into thousands of stars.
M23: A rich open cluster set against the Milky Way in Sagittarius.
M24: Not a cluster at all but a window: a gap in the dust that lets us look thousands of light years into a spiral arm of our own galaxy.
M25: A bright, loose open cluster containing a Cepheid variable, which is what fixed its distance.
M26: A modest open cluster with a curious sparse region near its centre, probably dust in front of it.
M27: The Dumbbell Nebula, the first planetary nebula ever found. It is a sun-like star's outer layers, thrown off and lit by the white dwarf left behind.
M28: A compact globular cluster close to the galactic centre, and one of the first places a millisecond pulsar was found.
M29: A small, loose group of hot young stars in Cygnus, dimmed by the dust of the galactic plane it sits in.
M30: A globular cluster whose core has collapsed, leaving an extremely dense centre.
M31: The Andromeda Galaxy, the nearest large spiral and the most distant thing most people can see without a telescope. It is heading towards us, and the two galaxies will merge.
M32: A small, very dense elliptical companion of Andromeda, probably the stripped remains of a larger galaxy.
M33: The Triangulum Galaxy, face on and full of star forming regions. Its low surface brightness makes it far harder to see than its magnitude suggests.
M34: A bright, loose open cluster of a few hundred million years old, well suited to a wide field.
M35: A large, rich open cluster with a much older and more distant cluster, NGC 2158, apparently beside it.
M36: The smallest and youngest of the three open clusters in Auriga, made of hot blue stars.
M37: The richest of the Auriga clusters, a dense sprinkling of stars with a red giant near the middle.
M38: An open cluster whose brighter stars are often described as forming a rough cross or the Greek letter pi.
M39: A very loose, very near open cluster, better in binoculars than in a telescope.
M40: A mistake that stayed in the catalogue: Messier looked for a nebula reported here, found only a double star, and listed it anyway.
M41: A bright open cluster a few degrees below Sirius, with several orange giants among its stars. Aristotle may have recorded it.
M42: The nearest region of massive star formation, and the brightest nebula in the sky. Four young stars at its heart, the Trapezium, light the whole cloud.
M43: Part of the same cloud as the Orion Nebula, separated from it only by a lane of dust in front.
M44: The Beehive, one of the nearest open clusters. It is a naked eye smudge that Galileo was the first to resolve into stars.
M45: The Pleiades. A young cluster passing through an unrelated dust cloud, which is what the blue haze around the brightest stars is.
M46: A rich open cluster with a planetary nebula apparently inside it. The two are not related: the nebula is much closer to us.
M47: A bright, loose cluster next to M46 in the sky, and much nearer. Messier recorded its position wrong and it was lost for two centuries.
M48: A large open cluster that Messier also misplaced, so it too spent a long time listed as missing.
M49: A giant elliptical, the brightest galaxy in the Virgo Cluster and the first member of it to be found.
M50: An open cluster often described as heart shaped, with a red giant standing out against its blue stars.
M51: The Whirlpool, the first galaxy recognised as having spiral arms. It is pulling a smaller companion apart, which is what makes the arms so sharp.
M52: A rich open cluster in Cassiopeia, a short hop from the Bubble Nebula in the same field.
M53: A globular cluster well out from the galactic centre, with a very loose companion cluster nearby.
M54: It looks like an ordinary globular, but it belongs to a small galaxy the Milky Way is swallowing, which makes it the first extragalactic globular found.
M55: A large, loose globular that resolves into stars readily, low in the south for most northern observers.
M56: A modest globular set against a rich Milky Way field between Albireo and the Ring Nebula.
M57: The Ring Nebula, the textbook planetary. What looks like a smoke ring is a shell of gas seen from the end, lit by the dying star at its centre.
M58: A barred spiral in the Virgo Cluster, one of the few barred galaxies Messier catalogued.
M59: An elliptical galaxy in the Virgo Cluster, rotating the opposite way to its own inner stars.
M60: A giant elliptical with an enormous black hole, apparently touching a face on spiral that lies behind it.
M61: A face on barred spiral and one of the most prolific producers of supernovae known, which keeps it under watch.
M62: A globular cluster badly distorted by its closeness to the galactic centre, with a core well off to one side.
M63: The Sunflower Galaxy, whose arms break into many short flocculent segments rather than two grand sweeps.
M64: The Black Eye Galaxy, named for the dark dust band across its core. Its gas rotates the opposite way to its stars, the remains of a galaxy it absorbed.
M65: One of the Leo Triplet, a spiral seen at a steep angle with a prominent dust lane.
M66: The brightest of the Leo Triplet, with arms visibly distorted by its neighbours.
M67: One of the oldest open clusters known, about the age of the Sun and still held together, which most clusters are not.
M68: A globular cluster in the far south of Hydra, well away from the crowded galactic centre.
M69: A small, metal rich globular close to the galactic centre, discovered by Lacaille from the Cape.
M70: A compact globular that happened to be in the field when comet Hale-Bopp was discovered in 1995.
M71: A very loose globular that spent decades classified as a dense open cluster before the argument was settled.
M72: One of the faintest and most distant globulars in the Messier catalogue.
M73: Four unrelated stars that line up by chance. Messier listed the group as a cluster with nebulosity; there is neither.
M74: The Phantom Galaxy, a perfect face on spiral. Its light is spread so thinly that it is one of the hardest Messier objects to see.
M75: One of the most distant and most concentrated globulars in the catalogue.
M76: The Little Dumbbell, the faintest planetary nebula Messier listed, shaped by a ring of gas seen edge on.
M77: A barred spiral with an intensely bright core, and the prototype of the Seyfert galaxies: an active black hole is feeding at its centre.
M78: The brightest reflection nebula in the sky. It shines by scattered starlight rather than by glowing itself, which is why it is blue.
M79: A globular that probably does not belong to our galaxy at all, but to a small one the Milky Way is absorbing.
M80: One of the densest globulars in the galaxy. A nova flared in it in 1860 and briefly outshone the whole cluster.
M81: Bode's Galaxy, a grand design spiral and one of the brightest galaxies in the sky. It is the head of a group that includes M82.
M82: The Cigar Galaxy, torn up by a close pass with M81. Star formation is running so hard that gas is being blown out of the middle in a red plume.
M83: The Southern Pinwheel, a barred spiral seen face on and one of the most photogenic galaxies in the sky.
M84: A lenticular galaxy at one end of Markarian's Chain, a curving string of galaxies through the heart of the Virgo Cluster.
M85: The northernmost galaxy of the Virgo Cluster, a lenticular with signs of a merger in its past.
M86: Unusually, it is coming towards us. It is falling through the Virgo Cluster fast enough that its gas is being stripped away behind it.
M87: A giant elliptical with a jet thousands of light years long. The black hole at its centre was the first ever imaged, in 2019.
M88: A multi-armed spiral seen at an angle, one of the brightest in the Virgo Cluster.
M89: The roundest elliptical known, though a faint envelope of gas stretches well beyond the visible galaxy.
M90: One of the few galaxies approaching us, moving fast enough through the Virgo Cluster to have had its gas stripped out.
M91: A barred spiral and the faintest object in the Messier catalogue. Messier recorded it wrongly and it was not identified again until 1969.
M92: A superb globular that would be famous anywhere else in the sky, and is overlooked only because M13 is in the same constellation.
M93: A bright, wedge shaped open cluster of a few hundred stars.
M94: A spiral with a bright inner ring of young stars around its core, and a much fainter outer ring beyond.
M95: A barred spiral with a ring of star formation around the core, one of the Leo I group.
M96: The brightest galaxy in the Leo I group, with arms pulled asymmetric by its neighbours.
M97: The Owl Nebula, named for the two dark hollows in it that look like eyes. They are holes in a barrel shaped shell, seen from the end.
M98: A nearly edge on spiral in the Virgo Cluster, approaching us rather than receding.
M99: A face on spiral with one arm pulled out longer than the rest, the mark of a close pass with another galaxy.
M100: One of the brightest spirals in the Virgo Cluster, and one of the first galaxies used to measure the expansion rate of the universe.
M101: The Pinwheel Galaxy, large, face on and asymmetric, with its core noticeably off centre.
M102: The only Messier object whose identity is still argued over. It is usually taken to be the Spindle Galaxy, an edge on lenticular with a sharp dust lane.
M103: A small, distant open cluster shaped like a fan, with a bright red giant among its stars.
M104: The Sombrero, an edge on galaxy with a dust lane so sharp it looks drawn on, and a huge glowing bulge behind it.
M105: An elliptical in the Leo I group with a well measured supermassive black hole at its centre.
M106: A spiral with two extra arms that glow in radio and X-rays rather than in starlight, driven by the active black hole at its core.
M107: The last globular added to the Messier catalogue, and one with unusual dark patches across it.
M108: An edge on barred spiral, mottled with dust and star forming regions, a short way from the Owl Nebula in the same field.
M109: A barred spiral with a strong, straight bar, the most distant galaxy in the Messier catalogue.
M110: A dwarf elliptical companion of Andromeda, and unusually for its kind it still contains dust and some young stars.
NGC7000: The North America Nebula, named for its shape. The dark lane that forms the Gulf of Mexico is foreground dust, not a gap in the cloud.
IC5070: The Pelican Nebula, part of the same cloud as the North America Nebula and separated from it only by the dust in front.
NGC7023: The Iris Nebula, a reflection nebula lit blue by a single hot star, set in a field of dark dust.
NGC6888: The Crescent Nebula, a shell blown by a Wolf-Rayet star shedding its outer layers before it goes supernova.
NGC6960: The western part of the Veil, the Witch's Broom, draped across the bright star 52 Cygni. It is a fragment of a supernova shell thousands of years old.
NGC6992: The eastern Veil, the brightest section of a supernova shell that has been expanding for around ten thousand years.
NGC6995: The Bat Nebula, part of the eastern Veil, where the shock front has broken into fine filaments.
NGC7635: The Bubble Nebula, a shell four hundredths of a degree across being inflated by the wind of one massive star inside it.
NGC281: The Pacman Nebula, named for the dark notch bitten out of it, which is a dust cloud lying in front.
NGC2237: The Rosette, a great ring of gas around a young cluster whose winds have cleared the middle.
IC434: The Horsehead, a pillar of cold dust silhouetted against the glowing hydrogen behind it. The shape will not last.
NGC2264: The Cone Nebula and the Christmas Tree Cluster, a single young star forming region seen in one field.
NGC1499: The California Nebula, a long ribbon of hydrogen lit by one nearby star, faint per unit area despite its size.
IC1396: A huge, faint emission nebula containing the Elephant's Trunk, a dark pillar being eroded by the radiation around it.
NGC7380: The Wizard Nebula, a young cluster still wrapped in the cloud that made it.
IC1805: The Heart Nebula, a large emission region shaped by the winds of the cluster at its centre.
IC1848: The Soul Nebula, next to the Heart and part of the same complex of star formation.
NGC253: The Sculptor Galaxy, a bright starburst spiral seen at a steep angle, and one of the easiest galaxies outside our own group.
NGC891: An almost perfectly edge on spiral, split lengthwise by a dust lane. It is thought to look much like our own galaxy from outside.
NGC4565: The Needle Galaxy, one of the thinnest edge on spirals in the sky, with a bulge that is a boxy bar seen end on.
NGC5128: Centaurus A, an elliptical with a broad dust lane across it, the wreckage of a spiral it swallowed. It is one of the brightest radio sources in the sky.
NGC3372: The Carina Nebula, one of the largest star forming regions known. It contains Eta Carinae, a star that nearly destroyed itself in the 1840s.
NGC2070: The Tarantula Nebula, in the Large Magellanic Cloud. It is so luminous that at the distance of the Orion Nebula it would cast shadows.
NGC104: 47 Tucanae, the second brightest globular cluster in the sky and one of the densest.
NGC5139: Omega Centauri, by far the largest globular cluster of the Milky Way, and probably the surviving core of a galaxy it absorbed.
NGC6302: The Bug Nebula, a planetary with two enormous lobes and one of the hottest central stars known, hidden behind a dust torus.
NGC7293: The Helix, one of the nearest planetary nebulae. The knots around its ring are each larger than our solar system.
NGC2392: A planetary nebula with a bright inner shell inside a fringed outer one, the outer layers of a sun-like star cast off a few thousand years ago.
NGC6543: The Cat's Eye, one of the most structurally complex planetary nebulae known, with a series of concentric shells around it.
NGC7331: A spiral much like the Milky Way, with a group of far more distant galaxies apparently beside it.
NGC6822: Barnard's Galaxy, a small irregular in our own Local Group, close enough that its individual star forming regions can be picked out.
IC342: A large face on spiral hidden behind the dust of the Milky Way, which is the only reason it is not one of the famous galaxies.
NGC1333: A reflection nebula over a dense cloud where low mass stars are forming right now.
NGC869: Half of the Double Cluster, two rich young clusters a few hundred light years apart and genuinely related.
NGC884: The other half of the Double Cluster, slightly the younger of the two.
SH2155: The Cave Nebula, an emission region with a dark arc across it that gives it its name.
NGC2244: The cluster at the centre of the Rosette Nebula, whose winds cleared the hole in the middle of it.
NGC7789: Caroline's Rose, a rich old open cluster whose star lanes and gaps suggest the petals of a flower.
NGC457: The Owl or E.T. Cluster, with two bright stars as eyes and lines of fainter stars as outstretched arms.
